Tides are one of the most reliable and fascinating rhythms in the natural world, and they happen because of the gravitational pull exerted by the moon and, to a lesser extent, the sun on the Earth's oceans. The moon, being our closest celestial neighbor, has the strongest influence. As the moon orbits the Earth, its gravity pulls on the water covering the planet's surface, drawing it toward the side of the Earth that faces the moon. This creates a bulge of water, known as a tidal bulge, which we experience as a high tide.

What many people find surprising is that there is a second bulge on the opposite side of the Earth as well. This happens because the moon's gravity pulls the solid Earth slightly toward it too, but the water on the far side is left behind, effectively creating a second high tide on the side facing away from the moon. The result is that most coastal areas experience two high tides and two low tides roughly every twenty-four hours and fifty minutes, which accounts for the moon's slow orbital movement around our planet each day.

The sun also plays a role, though its influence is about half that of the moon because of its much greater distance. When the sun, moon, and Earth align during new and full moons, their combined gravitational forces produce especially high high tides and especially low low tides, known as spring tides. When the sun and moon are at right angles to each other during the first and third quarters of the lunar cycle, their pulls partially cancel out, leading to more moderate tides called neap tides.
